title: Targets carry their own requirements
summary: Declare an executable and attach its language standard and include path to the target.

scenario.briefing: The campus inventory tool builds only on one laptop because its include path and C++ standard are set globally. Declare the project and attach both requirements to the executable.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.

hints: Call project() once, right after cmake_minimum_required.
add_executable already names the target inventory.
Attach the standard with target_compile_features(inventory PRIVATE cxx_std_20).
Attach the include path with target_include_directories(inventory PRIVATE include).

misconceptions.description: Using include_directories for a path only one target needs.
misconceptions.testDescription: The project is declared after the minimum version.
misconceptions.feedback: Global include paths apply to every target in the directory and hide which target needs the headers. Attach the path with target_include_directories.

misconceptions.description: Setting CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD globally because it is shorter.
misconceptions.testDescription: The standard and include path belong to the target.
misconceptions.feedback: A global standard forces every target in the tree, including third-party code, onto one mode. target_compile_features states the requirement per target.

misconceptions.diagnostic: Selecting the statement that add_executable must run before project().
misconceptions.feedback: project() declares the build and enables languages. Targets are created after it, not before.

sections.title: A target is the unit of build
sections.body: CMake describes targets, not files. add_executable creates an executable target from source files, and every later requirement names that target so it can be applied to exactly one build product.

sections.title: Requirements flow through usage
sections.body: target_compile_features records the language standard as a requirement of the target. target_include_directories adds an include path to the target's compile line, and PRIVATE keeps it out of the interface seen by consumers.

steps.title: Declare a CMake target
steps.prompt: Edit CMakeLists.txt. Set the minimum CMake version and project, create the inventory executable, and attach the C++20 requirement and include directory to that target.

files.content:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.24)

add_executable(inventory src/main.cpp)

# TODO: declare the project and move the include path onto the target
include_directories(include)

steps.title: CMake target semantics

statements.label: project() names the build and selects the languages it enables.
cmake_minimum_required should appear before project() so policies are set early.
A global include path affects every target in the directory, including unrelated ones.
target_compile_features attaches a language-standard requirement to one target.
add_executable must be called before project().
PRIVATE include directories still become part of a consumer's interface.

steps.explanation: A CMake build is a graph of targets. The minimum version and project declare the policy baseline and enabled languages; add_executable creates a build product; target_compile_features and target_include_directories attach requirements to that product only. Global commands like include_directories leak flags into unrelated targets, which makes builds fragile.
hints: Check which commands attach requirements to a target instead of a directory.
A target is the unit that carries usage requirements.
Global include paths affect every target in the directory.
PRIVATE requirements are not published to consumers.
